$comment: Ground truth for the RECALL threshold sweep. spec/03-MEMORY-MODEL.md §4.1.
Written by hand on 2026-08-12 BEFORE anything was embedded or measured, which is
the same discipline bench/tasks.json's `pair` labels were written under. If this
file is ever edited after seeing a sweep result, the sweep stops being evidence
and becomes a fit.
The relation being declared is not similarity. It is: *an agent is about to do
this task — does the fleet already hold something that bears on it?* Every
finding below is an honest wording of what an agent would record after finishing
a piece of work in bench/tasks.json, not a restatement of the task itself.
Each query declares `relevant`. Every (query, finding) pair NOT listed there is a
declared negative — the grid is total, 8 queries × 22 findings = 176 decided
cells, so a threshold cannot score well by being vague.
`arguable` names the pairs where the call is genuinely debatable in either
direction. Recall relevance is fuzzier than dedupe equivalence — 'is this the
same work' has an answer, 'does this bear on my work' has a judgement — and
pretending otherwise would overstate the result. The sweep reports the band under
these calls and again under every arguable call flipped, so a reader can see how
much of the answer rests on judgement.
Three findings carry a measured distance in `note`. Those are V28's numbers,
recorded in docs/SPEC-DELTA.md before this file existed, and they are the reason
the sweep is being run at all.

findings.fact: the orders-by-customer index covers customer_id only, so history reads still sort in memory
creating the orders-by-customer index needed a backfill window — it went in NOT VISIBLE first
the payment charge is idempotent on the request key, which is stored on the charge row
one request key reused across charge and refund collided — keys must be namespaced per operation
monetary amounts are integer minor units; the float columns were dropped after a two-step backfill
rounding half-up when converting floats to minor units lost a cent on refunds and was reverted
adding a retry to the orders client broke 429 handling and was reverted
findings.note: V28 measured this at 0.3801 from 'add a retry to the orders client' — the closest of six honest wordings, and still outside 0.35.

findings.fact: orders client retry: skip 429
a retry in the orders client must skip 429 — retrying it drops the order
rate limiting login by IP alone locked out a shared office network and was reverted
the login rate limiter keys on account plus IP
a blanket five second outbound timeout broke the report export, which legitimately takes twenty
the order list endpoint paginates by offset, which skips rows under concurrent inserts
order status transitions are recorded in their own table, not derived from the orders row
SMS delivery-failure retries flooded the carrier until they were capped at three attempts
inventory availability is cached for thirty seconds, which is stale enough to oversell
shipping address validation rejected valid PO boxes and had to be loosened
expiring idle sessions at thirty minutes logged users out mid-checkout
the logger loses the request id when the worker forks
raising the password hashing cost factor doubled sign-in latency at the p99
shipping quotes were cached for thirty seconds and went stale after a carrier rate change
order confirmation emails double-sent when the placement handler retried

queries.statement: Build a customer order history view on top of the customer lookup index
queries.why: R1 declares dependsOn C4, so C4's two findings are the declared case. FC1a is called relevant because a history view is a list and the fleet already learned offset pagination skips rows — that is a lesson transferring within a subsystem. FC2a is refused: order *status* history is different work from a customer's order history, and it shares only the word.

queries.statement: Extend the refund path with the same request key handling the charge path uses
queries.why: R2 declares dependsOn P3a. FP3b is the load-bearing one — it names the exact collision this task walks into. FI3b is called relevant because it is a recorded revert on the refund path, which is the path being edited.

queries.statement: Convert stored shipping quotes to the new integer minor unit representation
queries.why: R3 declares dependsOn I3. FSQ1 is refused despite being the only other finding about shipping quotes: quote *caching* has nothing to do with the unit representation, and admitting it would mean the subsystem name alone earns a recall.

queries.statement: add a retry to the orders client
queries.why: The demo's own beat-1 query, and V28's measured case. FI4a is refused: it shares the word retry and the shape of the lesson, but SMS carrier throttling is not the orders client, and a fleet that recalls it here is recalling on vocabulary.

queries.statement: Add rate limiting to the login endpoint
queries.why: FP5a is refused: session expiry and rate limiting are both auth-adjacent and both about a thirty-minute-ish window, which is exactly why it is the hard negative rather than an easy one.

queries.statement: Apply a five second timeout to every outbound HTTP request
queries.why: FI4a and FOC2 are refused. Both concern outbound calls failing and being retried, which is adjacent to a timeout policy without bearing on it — the timeout task needs to know which callers legitimately run long, and neither says.

queries.statement: Cache inventory availability lookups for thirty seconds
queries.why: FSQ1 is called relevant and it is the most interesting cell in this file: a thirty-second cache that went stale after an upstream rate change is the same trap in a different subsystem. Cross-subsystem transfer is a large part of what shared memory is for, and it is the first thing a tight threshold destroys.

queries.statement: Send an order confirmation email when an order is placed
queries.why: A clean case with one obvious answer, included so the corpus is not made entirely of hard ones.
